title: Getting Dressed
subtext: For when your toddler refuses clothes, runs away, or melts down
script: I can see you don't want to get dressed. It's time to get ready now. Do you want to put on your shirt first or your pants first?
steps: Get down to their level (eye contact)
Say the script calmly, once
Offer a simple choice (shirt or pants first)
Pause and wait — don't repeat
Gently guide if they don't choose
avoid: Arguing or explaining too much
Repeating the request over and over
Giving big open-ended choices ('What do you want to wear?')
Giving in after saying no
resist: I won't let you stay in pyjamas. I'm going to help you get dressed.
resist_note: Calmly guide them into the first step (e.g. shirt)
tip_headline: Smaller choices = less resistance
tip_instead_of: What do you want to wear?
tip_try: Blue shirt or red shirt?

title: Hitting
subtext: For when they strike out at you, a sibling, or another child
script: I won’t let you hit. Hitting hurts.
steps: Block or gently hold thier hands
Stay calm and firm
Keep your body between them and others
Reconnect warmly once they're calm
avoid: Yelling or hitting back
Long explanations in the heat of the moment
Ignoring it completely
resist: Hands are not for hitting. If you're angry, you can stomp your feet or say 'I'm mad'.
resist_note: Stay close, speak quietly, keep your body relaxed
tip_headline: Stay physically calm and neutral—your reaction teaches what’s acceptable.
tip_instead_of: Trying to talk them through it in the moment
tip_try: Focus on stopping the behaviour first, then talk once they’re calm

title: Bedtime Refusal
subtext: For when they won’t settle, keep getting up, or resist going to bed
script: It’s bedtime now. You can walk yourself to bed or I can guide you.
steps: Keep lights low and voice calm
Say the script once, clearly
Guide them to bed if needed
Keep interactions minimal
Repeat consistently if they get up
avoid: Negotiating extra time
Long conversations or reasoning
Introducing new activities
Inconsistent responses
resist: It’s time to sleep. I’m here. Your body needs rest.
resist_note: Stay calm, keep your voice low, and avoid engaging further
tip_headline: Boring = effective at bedtime.
tip_instead_of: Talking or engaging when they get up
tip_try: Keep responses short and repeat the same calm phrase

title: Leaving the House
subtext: For when getting out the door turns into a battle
script: We’re going now. Shoes on first, then we go outside.
steps: Give a clear, simple sequence
Say it once, calmly
Start the first step immediately
Keep momentum moving
Guide physically if needed
avoid: Giving multiple instructions at once
Waiting too long after saying it’s time
Turning it into a discussion
Showing frustration
resist: We’re leaving now. I’m going to help you get ready.
resist_note: Stay calm and move them gently into action
tip_headline: Clarity reduces resistance.
tip_instead_of: “Come on, we’re going!”
tip_try: “Shoes on, then outside.”

title: Leaving the Park
subtext: For when they don’t want to leave and emotions run high
script: I know you want to stay. It’s time to go now. Do you want to walk or be carried?
steps: Acknowledge their feeling
Give two clear options
Pause briefly
Follow through calmly
Stay consistent
avoid: Surprising them with no warning
Saying “just one more” repeatedly
Negotiating after saying it’s time
Rushing without connection
resist: You can't stay. I’m going to help you go now.
resist_note: Stay calm and carry them if needed without adding extra words
tip_headline: Transitions work better with a heads-up.
tip_instead_of: Ending play suddenly
tip_try: “2 more minutes, then we’re leaving.”

title: Food Refusal
subtext: For when they refuse food or push meals away
script: This is dinner. You don’t have to eat, but this is what’s available.
steps: Serve the meal calmly
Let them decide how much to eat
Keep the atmosphere neutral
Avoid pressure or attention on eating
End the meal without stress
avoid: Forcing bites
Making separate meals immediately
Turning it into a power struggle
Praising or pressuring too much
resist: Dinner is finished. You can eat more next time.
resist_note: Stay neutral and move on without extending the moment
tip_headline: Less pressure = more willingness over time.
tip_instead_of: “Just take one bite”
tip_try: Stay neutral and let them choose
Having multiple options on the plate

title: Won’t Listen
subtext: For when they ignore instructions or don’t respond
script: (name), I need you to listen. It’s time to (instruction).
steps: Get close and at their level
Say their name first
Give one clear instruction
Pause and wait
Follow through if needed
avoid: Calling from across the room
Repeating instructions multiple times
Giving multiple steps at once
Raising your voice
resist: I’m going to help you now.
resist_note: Gently guide them to complete the task
tip_headline: Connection improves cooperation.
tip_instead_of: Repeating yourself louder
tip_try: Get close, say their name, then give the instruction

title: Won't Stay in Bed
subtext: For when they keep getting out of bed after lights out
script: It's time to stay in bed now. Every time you get up, I'm going to bring you straight back. I love you. Goodnight.
steps: Say goodnight warmly but briefly — don't linger
The first time they get up, return them silently with minimal interaction
Each return after that: no eye contact, no talking, just guide them back
Be completely boring — no negotiation, no extra cuddles, no conversation
Stay consistent even if it takes many returns — it will reduce over nights
avoid: Engaging in conversation each time they come out
Allowing 'one more' of anything — drink, hug, question
Raising your voice or showing frustration
Giving up and letting them stay up — it resets the pattern
resist: Back to bed. I'll see you in the morning. I love you.
resist_note: Say it once, quietly, then guide them back without further words
tip_headline: Boring = faster
tip_instead_of: Okay fine, just five more minutes in our bed
tip_try: Silent return, every time — consistency is the only thing that works

title: Throwing Food
subtext: For when food gets thrown instead of eaten
script: Food stays on the table. If you throw it again, I'm going to take your plate away and mealtime will be finished.
steps: Stay calm — a big reaction makes throwing more interesting
State the boundary once, clearly
If they throw again, calmly remove the plate without drama
Don't replace the meal or offer alternatives
Try again at the next mealtime as if nothing happened
avoid: Laughing or reacting dramatically — it encourages repetition
Repeatedly warning without following through
Making them feel ashamed or bad about themselves
Turning mealtime into a long battle
resist: Plate's gone for now. We'll try again at dinner.
resist_note: Remove calmly, clean up without fuss, move on with the day
tip_headline: Reaction is the reward — remove it
tip_instead_of: Stop that! Don't throw your food! How many times do I have to say it?
tip_try: Food stays on the table. (remove plate if it happens) Done for now.

title: Only Wants Snacks
subtext: For when they refuse meals but keep asking for snacks
script: Snacks are finished for now. The next time we eat is dinner. I know that's hard to wait for.
steps: Set clear snack times and stick to them
Serve meals first — no snacks within 1.5 hours of a meal
Don't negotiate or explain at length when they ask
Acknowledge the frustration without giving in
Trust that a hungry child will eat at the next meal
avoid: Offering snacks to avoid a meltdown right before a meal
Caving because they 'didn't eat enough' at the last meal
Making separate snack meals as a replacement for dinner
Turning it into a long conversation about nutrition
resist: I hear you — you're hungry. Dinner is in 30 minutes and that's when we eat next.
resist_note: Offer water, then divert attention to an activity
tip_headline: Hunger is not an emergency — it's a signal
tip_instead_of: Fine, just a few crackers to tide you over
tip_try: Dinner is at 5:30. That's when the kitchen opens next.

title: Refuses to Sit at Table
subtext: For when they won't stay seated during meals
script: When you leave the table, mealtime is finished. Do you want to stay and keep eating, or are you done?
steps: Set the expectation before the meal, not during it
Keep mealtimes short — toddlers don't need to sit for 30 minutes
If they leave, let them — don't chase or coax them back
No more food until the next meal if they choose to leave
Make sitting together pleasant so they want to stay
avoid: Chasing them around with food
Letting them graze standing up after leaving the table
Extending mealtime trying to get them to eat more
Forcing them back into the seat physically
resist: You've left the table so mealtime is done. That's okay — we'll eat again at snack time.
resist_note: Follow through calmly — the boundary only works if it's real
tip_headline: Short meals with clear endings beat long battles
tip_instead_of: Come back! You haven't eaten enough! Just sit down for two more minutes!
tip_try: We sit at the table while we eat. Ready to come back, or are you all done?

title: Screaming / Yelling
subtext: For when they shout loudly instead of communicating
script: That's a really loud voice. I can hear you want something. Can you show me with your quiet voice or your hands?
steps: Don't match their volume — stay noticeably quieter than them
Acknowledge that they want something without giving in to the scream
Ask for a quieter version of the same request
When they use a quieter voice, respond immediately and warmly
Check if they're overtired or overwhelmed — screaming is often a signal
avoid: Screaming back or matching their intensity
Giving them what they want while they're screaming
Shushing aggressively — it often escalates
Ignoring completely if they're genuinely distressed
resist: I'm going to wait until your voice is quieter. I'm right here.
resist_note: Pause, stay calm, and wait — respond the moment the volume drops
tip_headline: Your quiet voice is louder than theirs
tip_instead_of: Stop screaming! USE YOUR WORDS!
tip_try: Ooh, that's a big voice. Can I hear your small voice? What do you need?

title: Crying Over Small Things
subtext: For when minor issues lead to big tears
script: I can see that really upset you. It's okay to feel sad about that. I'm here.
steps: Resist the urge to minimise it — 'it's not a big deal' shuts them down
Name the feeling without judgement
Sit with them briefly rather than trying to fix it fast
Let the feeling pass naturally — don't prolong it with lots of attention
Move on warmly once they've settled
avoid: "You're fine" or "Stop crying" or "That's nothing to cry about"
Laughing at the reason they're upset
Over-comforting in a way that prolongs the crying
Problem-solving before they feel heard
resist: You really wanted that to go differently. That's okay. Take your time.
resist_note: Stay nearby without too much fuss — presence without prolonging
tip_headline: To them, it IS a big deal — meet them there first
tip_instead_of: Seriously? You're crying over that? It's just a cracker.
tip_try: Oh, that was really disappointing wasn't it. I get it. (sit quietly)

title: Overstimulation Meltdown
subtext: For when too much noise, activity, or change leads to overwhelm
script: There's a lot going on right now. Let's find a quiet spot together.
steps: Remove them from the environment if possible — even briefly
Reduce input: lower noise, dim lights, slow your movements
Say very little — your calm presence is enough
Don't try to talk them through it while it's happening
Give them time to regulate before returning to the activity
avoid: Telling them to calm down or pull themselves together
Introducing more stimulation (screens, toys, noise) to distract
Staying in the overwhelming environment and expecting them to cope
Rushing the recovery — they need as long as they need
resist: We're going to sit here quietly for a bit. No rush.
resist_note: Stay close, say little, breathe slowly — your nervous system regulates theirs
tip_headline: Prevention beats recovery — watch for the build-up
tip_instead_of: You were fine five minutes ago! What happened?
tip_try: (move to quieter space, sit down, say nothing — just be there)

title: Separation Anxiety
subtext: For when they struggle to be apart from you
script: I'm going now and I will be back at [specific time]. I love you. Bye bye.
steps: Give a specific, concrete return time they can understand
Keep the goodbye short and confident — don't linger
Don't sneak out — it damages trust and worsens anxiety long term
Say goodbye once, warmly, and then go
Trust the carer — most children settle within minutes of you leaving
avoid: Sneaking out to avoid the tears
Returning because they're upset — it reinforces that crying brings you back
Long drawn-out goodbyes that escalate the anxiety
Saying "I'll only be a minute" if that's not true
resist: I know it's hard. I love you. I'll be back after your nap.
resist_note: Say it once, mean it, then leave — hesitation makes it harder
tip_headline: Confident goodbyes create secure children
tip_instead_of: Are you sure you'll be okay? Maybe I should stay a bit longer...
tip_try: Big hug. I love you. Back at 3 o'clock. Bye! (then go)

title: Clinginess
subtext: For when they won't let you out of their sight
script: I'm just going to [specific place] to do [specific thing]. I'll be back in two minutes. You can come find me.
steps: Always tell them where you're going — never just disappear
Give a concrete, short timeframe
Follow through and return when you said you would
Build trust through small, successful separations
Make sure their connection cup is full — more quality time often reduces clinginess
avoid: Sneaking away when they're distracted
Getting frustrated or calling them 'too clingy'
Pushing them away when they reach for you
Ignoring the underlying need for connection
resist: I hear you — you want to be close. I'm coming right back. Two minutes.
resist_note: Return when you said you would — every kept promise builds independence
tip_headline: More connection now = more independence later
tip_instead_of: Stop following me everywhere! I just need five minutes to myself!
tip_try: I'm going to the kitchen. I'll be back before you count to ten.

title: Throwing Objects
subtext: For when toys or items are thrown during play or frustration
script: Toys aren't for throwing. If you throw it again, I'm going to put it away for the rest of the day.
steps: State the boundary calmly and once
If they throw again, remove the object immediately without drama
Don't return the object for the rest of that play session
Offer a safe alternative if they need to throw: a soft ball outside
Reconnect once they're calm — no lingering punishment
avoid: Throwing things back to show them how it feels
Warning repeatedly without following through
Long lectures about safety while they're dysregulated
Making them feel like a bad person
resist: That toy is done for today. We can try again tomorrow.
resist_note: Remove it calmly and redirect — don't extend the moment
tip_headline: Give them somewhere safe to throw — outside with a ball
tip_instead_of: How many times do I have to tell you not to throw things?!
tip_try: We don't throw toys. (remove it) Want to throw the ball outside instead?

title: Climbing Unsafe Things
subtext: For when they climb furniture or unsafe spaces
script: That's not safe to climb. I'm going to help your body get down. You can climb at the park.
steps: Move to them calmly — don't shout from across the room
Help them down physically if needed, without anger
Name a safe alternative immediately
Childproof where possible — remove the temptation
Get them to a place where climbing IS allowed regularly
avoid: Shouting from a distance — it startles and can cause falls
Shaming them for their natural impulse to climb
Removing all climbing opportunities — they need to climb
Long explanations while they're mid-climb
resist: I'm going to help you down now. Bodies aren't safe up there.
resist_note: Guide them down firmly but gently — stay calm so they do too
tip_headline: Climbing is healthy — redirect to where it's safe
tip_instead_of: GET DOWN FROM THERE RIGHT NOW! You're going to hurt yourself!
tip_try: Down we come. (help them) Let's find somewhere safe to climb.

title: Running Away
subtext: For when they bolt in public or unsafe areas
script: Stop. Hold my hand. It's not safe to run here.
steps: Use a firm, calm voice — not panicked, not angry
Catch up and hold their hand or put them in the pram/carrier
Keep the explanation brief — their brain can't process lectures mid-bolt
Praise them clearly when they do walk well
Use reins or a wrist strap in high-risk environments without guilt
avoid: Chasing them while laughing — it becomes a game
Shouting from a distance and expecting compliance
Extended explanations about danger while still outside
Shaming them in front of others
resist: Hand please. We hold hands in the carpark. That's the rule.
resist_note: Take their hand firmly — this is a safety boundary, not a negotiation
tip_headline: Use reins without guilt — safety comes first
tip_instead_of: Come back here! Stop running! Do you have any idea how dangerous that is?!
tip_try: Stop. (catch up) Hand. Thank you. We hold hands here.

title: Snatching
subtext: For when they grab toys or items from others
script: You snatched that from her. Let's give it back and ask properly. Can you say — can I have a turn?
steps: Step in quickly but calmly
Return the item to the other child first
Coach them to ask instead — keep it simple
Stay close to support rather than walking away
Praise any moment of waiting or asking nicely
avoid: Forcing a hug or sorry that isn't genuine
Long lectures about sharing while they're frustrated
Dismissing the other child's upset
Letting it go to keep the peace — it repeats
resist: We're going to give that back and then ask. I'll help you.
resist_note: Coach the words — 'can I have a turn?' — then wait together
tip_headline: Coach the ask — don't just correct the snatch
tip_instead_of: That was so naughty! Say sorry RIGHT now!
tip_try: Let's give that back. Now ask: can I have a turn when you're done?

title: Screen Time Ending
subtext: For when turning off the TV or tablet triggers a meltdown
script: The show is going to finish in two minutes. When it's done, screens are done for now. What do you want to do after?
steps: Give a warning before the end — not during a critical moment
Use a timer they can see if possible
Turn it off yourself — don't ask them to do it
Have the next activity ready to move straight into
Stay neutral — no guilt, no lectures about screens
avoid: Saying 'one more episode' repeatedly
Turning it off mid-scene with no warning
Getting into a debate about screen time limits
Using screens as the only wind-down strategy
resist: I know you want to keep watching. Screens are done for now. Let's find something else.
resist_note: Don't re-open the negotiation — the boundary is the boundary
tip_headline: Transition activities beat cold turkey every time
tip_instead_of: Turn it off now! I said NOW!
tip_try: After this episode we're going to do (specific thing) — ready?

title: Getting Into Car Seat
subtext: For when they resist being strapped in
script: It's time to get in your seat. You can hold your toy or choose a song — but we need you buckled first.
steps: Give a small choice within the non-negotiable
Stay calm — urgency transfers to them and escalates resistance
If needed, guide them in physically without anger
Buckle efficiently once they're in — don't leave it half done
Acknowledge once you're moving: 'Thank you for getting in'
avoid: Bribing with screens every single time — it becomes the expectation
Forcing them in while you're visibly frustrated
Letting them ride unbuckled — this is a safety non-negotiable
Turning the car park into a long negotiation
resist: I'm going to help your body into the seat now. Here we go.
resist_note: Announce it, then do it calmly — no asking, just guiding
tip_headline: Car seat is never optional — your calm makes it faster
tip_instead_of: Get in the seat RIGHT NOW or we're not going anywhere!
tip_try: Hop in and you can pick the music. In you go.

title: Bath Time Resistance
subtext: For when they refuse or resist getting into the bath
script: Bath time now. Do you want to walk to the bathroom or shall I carry you like a rocket?
steps: Give a 5-minute warning before bath time starts
Offer a playful choice about how they get there
Make the bath itself appealing — toys, bubbles, glow sticks
Keep bath time consistent so it's predictable
Getting out can be just as tricky — warn before that too
avoid: Skipping baths repeatedly because of resistance — it gets harder
Making it a power struggle by demanding compliance
Threatening consequences for not getting in
Rushing them — bath time is often also wind-down time
resist: In the bath we go. I'll help your body. There we are.
resist_note: Guide them in warmly — once they're in, most children relax quickly
tip_headline: The transition is the hard part — make it playful
tip_instead_of: Get in the bath NOW. I'm not asking again.
tip_try: Bath time! Rocket ship or piggyback to the bathroom?

title: Interrupting Adults
subtext: For when they constantly interrupt conversations
script: I can see you need me. Put your hand on my arm and I'll know you're waiting. I'll come to you as soon as I can.
steps: Teach the hand-on-arm signal before you need it, not mid-conversation
Acknowledge their hand quickly so they know it works
Finish your thought, then turn to them promptly
Thank them for waiting — even imperfect waiting
Keep adult conversations short when toddlers are nearby
avoid: Ignoring them completely — they'll escalate until heard
Snapping at them for interrupting without teaching an alternative
Expecting long waits — their impulse control is genuinely limited
Inconsistency — letting it go sometimes and correcting other times
resist: I see your hand. I'm coming in just a moment. Thank you for waiting.
resist_note: Acknowledge the signal quickly or they'll lose trust in it
tip_headline: Teach the signal before the situation — not during it
tip_instead_of: Can't you see I'm talking?! Just wait!
tip_try: Put your hand here (on your arm) and I'll know you need me.

title: Brushing Teeth
subtext: For when they refuse or resist tooth brushing
script: It's tooth brushing time. Do you want to do it first or shall I do it first?
steps: Let them brush first — then you do the 'grown-up' brush after
Make it quick — 2 minutes feels long, use a timer or song
Let them choose their toothbrush and toothpaste flavour
Stay consistent — every night, no exceptions
If they clamp shut, stay calm and try again — don't skip it
avoid: Skipping it to avoid the battle — it becomes harder each time
Pinning them down without warning
Turning it into a lengthy negotiation
Bribing with sweet things — counterproductive
resist: I'm going to brush your teeth now. Open wide — I'll be quick.
resist_note: Be efficient — the faster it's done the less resistance builds
tip_headline: Let them go first — then you finish the job
tip_instead_of: Open your mouth RIGHT NOW or no story tonight!
tip_try: Your turn first! (let them brush) Now my turn to get the sneaky spots.

title: Taking Medicine
subtext: For when they refuse medicine or spit it out
script: This medicine is going to help your body feel better. You can have it from the spoon or the syringe — you pick.
steps: Give a choice of how, not whether
Mix with a small amount of food if safe to do so — check with your pharmacist
Follow immediately with something they like the taste of
Stay matter-of-fact — big reactions make it a bigger deal
Praise them after, even if it was a struggle
avoid: Hiding medicine without their knowledge if avoidable — trust matters
Making it a huge drama that primes resistance next time
Giving up if they spit it — note how much and re-dose appropriately
Forcing it in a way that makes them gag or panic
resist: I know you don't like it. It's still going to happen. Quick as we can.
resist_note: Stay calm and efficient — your confidence helps them comply
tip_headline: Choice of how, never choice of whether
tip_instead_of: Just take it! It's not that bad! Stop being so dramatic!
tip_try: Spoon or syringe? Quick or slow? You choose.

title: Sharing at Playdates
subtext: For when they struggle to share with other children
script: Before your friend arrives, let's put away the toys that are really special to you. Everything else is for sharing today.
steps: Do this before the playdate — not during the conflict
Let them choose 2-3 toys to put away safely
Everything else is fair game for the visit
Stay nearby to coach turn-taking rather than forcing sharing
Keep playdates short — they go better when everyone's still fresh
avoid: Forcing them to share toys that are genuinely precious to them
Shaming them in front of the other child or parent
Expecting toddlers to naturally share — it's a skill that develops over time
Staying out of it entirely and hoping for the best
resist: Let's take turns. You have it for two minutes, then it's her turn.
resist_note: Use a timer so the turn is concrete and predictable for both children
tip_headline: Pre-empt conflict by letting them protect what matters most
tip_instead_of: You HAVE to share! Don't be so selfish!
tip_try: Pick your special toys to put away. Everything else we share today.

title: Waiting Their Turn
subtext: For when they struggle with patience and waiting
script: It's not your turn yet. You're next. Let's count how many more sleeps — or let's watch her finish.
steps: Make the wait visible and concrete — a timer, counting, or watching
Stay close during the wait — don't walk away
Narrate the other person's turn: 'She's nearly done, then it's you'
Acknowledge how hard waiting is — it genuinely is hard for them
Celebrate when they manage it, even imperfectly
avoid: Expecting them to wait silently without support
Punishing them for struggling — impulse control is still developing
Letting them skip the queue to keep the peace
Minimising how hard it feels
resist: Still waiting. Nearly there. You're doing really well.
resist_note: Narrate the progress — give them something to hold onto
tip_headline: Make the wait visible — abstract waiting is hardest
tip_instead_of: Just WAIT. It's not your turn yet. Stop asking!
tip_try: You're next. Watch — when she gets off, you jump on.

title: Cleaning Up Toys
subtext: For when they refuse to tidy up after playing
script: It's tidy-up time. Let's see how fast we can do it together. Ready? Go!
steps: Make it a game or a race — toddlers respond to energy and fun
Do it with them, not just directing from afar
Use a consistent tidy-up song or signal
Keep it short — 5 minutes maximum at this age
Praise the effort, not just the result
avoid: Expecting them to do it all themselves
Threatening to throw toys away in anger
Making tidy-up such a battle that play becomes stressful
Doing it all yourself every time — they won't learn the habit
resist: I'll do the blocks, you do the cars. Let's go — together.
resist_note: Jump in alongside them — your participation makes them more likely to join
tip_headline: Together is always easier than directive
tip_instead_of: Pick all of this up RIGHT NOW before I throw it in the bin!
tip_try: Tidy-up time! Who can put the most things away in 60 seconds?
